claims.text: The starting AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy has a uniform, fine lamellar structure and contains no intentional Mo addition.
Adding approximately 2–3 at.% Mo during casting and applying solution treatment and aging at 700–750 °C will produce finely dispersed Mo-rich nanoprecipitates.
The Mo-rich nanoprecipitates will form preferentially at interlamellar boundaries.
Mo segregates to lamellar interfaces during solidification and subsequent heat treatment.
Interfacial Mo segregation leads to the formation of Mo-rich nanoprecipitates.
The Mo-rich nanoprecipitates obstruct dislocation motion.
The Mo-rich nanoprecipitates chemically stabilize the lamellar interfaces.
Obstructing dislocation motion and stabilizing the interfaces will improve the alloy's strength–ductility balance.
The Mo addition and resulting nanoprecipitates will improve room-temperature creep resistance relative to the Mo-free alloy.
The Mo addition and resulting nanoprecipitates will improve elevated-temperature creep resistance relative to the Mo-free alloy.
The Mo addition and chemical stabilization of the interfaces will increase corrosion resistance relative to the Mo-free alloy.
The original Mo-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy has insufficient long-term stability under mechanical loading, temperature fluctuations, and corrosive environments.
The predicted benefits depend on precise Mo doping and careful control of heat treatment within 700–750 °C.
Large heat-treatment deviations or inhomogeneous Mo distribution may prevent the desired nanoprecipitate structure and associated performance improvements.
Unoptimized processing may produce coarse or inhomogeneously distributed precipitates.
